title: How To Turn Around Difficult Students (Part 2)
author: Michael Linsin
summary: In the second installment of his series, Linsin introduces the 'members-only strategy' for the rare truly difficult student who remains unfazed by a solid classroom management plan. After confirming a teacher's own management fundamentals are sound and coordinating with parents and administration, the teacher moves the student's desk apart from the class and informs them they're temporarily not a full member of the classroom, still required to do schoolwork but excluded from group activities. For roughly the first week, the teacher leaves the student alone without lectures or pep talks, remaining pleasant but withholding verbal praise, while ramping up camaraderie and fun with the rest of the class. When the student shows signs of contrition, the teacher invites them to initiate rejoining the class; once they do so sincerely, the teacher welcomes them back without a warning or lecture and returns their desk to its normal place. Linsin frames the strategy as tapping into students' fundamental desire to belong.
points: The 'members-only strategy' is reserved for difficult students who remain unfazed by an otherwise solid, well-enforced classroom management plan.
Before starting, coordinate with the student's parents and school administrator, and begin the strategy on a Monday.
Move the student's desk apart from the class and inform them they're not a full member, though they must still complete regular schoolwork.
For about a week, leave the student alone without lectures or pep talks while remaining pleasant, and increase camaraderie with the rest of the class.
The student must initiate rejoining the class by approaching the teacher and showing genuine contrition; welcome them back without any added warning or lecture.
quotes: Most so-called difficult students need nothing more than a teacher with a solid classroom management plan and a thorough understanding of how to implement and enforce it.

Teachers who make decisions based on feeling sorry for students and their sometimes-awful circumstances can cause behavior to worsen. The most compassionate thing you can do for a difficult student is to hold him or her accountable.
When your students enter your classroom, pull the student in question aside and inform her that she is no longer a member of your classroom.
For the first week, leave Jennifer alone. No pep talks. No lectures. No profound words. Don’t tell her what to think or how to feel.
We all want to feel like we are part of something. No student is immune from this desire. This is why the more camaraderie, rapport, and fun you can create in your classroom the better.
She has to prove to you she’s ready. Does she talk about her mistakes? Does she apologize? Does she discuss how she is going to handle herself in the future?
After your conversation, move her desk back and let her rejoin her classmates as a member in good standing.
